1	# Global CO₂ Emissions: Who Emits, How Much, and What's Changing
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	https://ourworldindata.org/co2-emissions — Data from the Global Carbon Budget (2025). Authors: Hannah Ritchie and Max Roser.
     5	
     6	## Global Emission Trajectory
     7	
     8	Global CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels and industry have grown dramatically since the Industrial Revolution. Before industrialization, emissions were negligible. By 1950, the world emitted roughly 6 billion tonnes (Bt) of CO₂ per year. By 1990, this had nearly quadrupled to over 20 Bt. Today, global emissions exceed 35 Bt annually. While growth has slowed in recent years, emissions have not yet peaked.
     9	
    10	![Global CO₂ emissions over time](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    11	
    12	Emissions from land-use change have declined slightly in recent years, but fossil fuel emissions continue to dominate the total.
    13	
    14	## Regional and Country Shares
    15	
    16	The distribution of emissions has shifted profoundly over time. In 1900, Europe and the United States accounted for more than 90% of global CO₂ emissions. By 1950, they still represented over 85%. Today, they account for less than one-third. Asia — led by China — now dominates, producing roughly half of global emissions.
    17	
    18	![Share of global CO₂ emissions by country](./assets/figure_6.jpg)
    19	
    20	| Country / Region | Approx. Share of Global CO₂ (2024) | Trend |
    21	|---|---|---|
    22	| China | ~31% | Rising, growth slowing |
    23	| United States | ~13% | Declining |
    24	| India | ~8% | Rising |
    25	| European Union (27) | ~6% | Declining |
    26	| Russia | ~5% | Roughly stable |
    27	| Africa (total) | ~3–4% | Slowly rising |
    28	| South America (total) | ~3–4% | Roughly stable |
    29	| Int'l aviation & shipping | ~3% | Rising |
    30	
    31	Africa and South America each account for only 3–4% of global emissions — comparable to international aviation and shipping combined.
    32	
    33	## Per Capita Emissions and Inequality
    34	
    35	Per capita CO₂ emissions reveal stark global inequalities. The world's largest per capita emitters are major oil-producing nations with small populations (Qatar, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait). Among large, populous countries, the United States, Australia, and Canada have per capita emissions roughly three times the global average.
    36	
    37	![Per capita CO₂ emissions over time](./assets/figure_8.jpg)
    38	
    39	| Country | Per Capita CO₂ (approx. 2024) |
    40	|---|---|
    41	| United States | ~14 t |
    42	| Canada | ~14 t |
    43	| China | ~9 t |
    44	| South Africa | ~7 t |
    45	| European Union (27) | ~6 t |
    46	| World average | ~4.5 t |
    47	| United Kingdom | ~4 t |
    48	| India | ~2 t |
    49	| Kenya | ~0.4 t |
    50	| Chad / Niger | ~0.1 t |
    51	
    52	The gap is enormous: the average American or Australian emits in under two days what the average person in Mali or Niger emits in an entire year — a roughly 150x difference.
    53	
    54	Even among wealthy nations, per capita emissions vary significantly. France, the UK, and Portugal have much lower per capita emissions than Germany, the Netherlands, or the US, largely because a higher share of their electricity comes from nuclear and renewable sources rather than fossil fuels.
    55	
    56	## 2024 Annual Change
    57	
    58	The map of annual percentage change in CO₂ emissions for 2024 shows a mixed picture. Many Western nations — including the US, much of the EU, and the UK — saw emissions decline (shown in blue). Meanwhile, Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations experienced increases (shown in orange and red). Some countries in Central Asia (e.g., Turkmenistan/Uzbekistan region) saw particularly large increases exceeding 10%.
    59	
    60	![Annual percentage change in CO₂ emissions, 2024](./assets/figure_5.jpg)
    61	
    62	## Key Findings
    63	
    64	- **No peak yet**: Global CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels exceed 35 billion tonnes per year and have not yet peaked, despite slowing growth.
    65	- **Dramatic shift in responsibility**: Europe and the US dominated emissions historically (>90% in 1900) but now account for less than one-third; China alone emits over a quarter of the global total.
    66	- **Massive per capita inequality**: A 150x gap exists between the lowest emitters (Sub-Saharan Africa, ~0.1 t/person) and the highest large-country emitters (US/Canada/Australia, ~14–15 t/person).
    67	- **Energy policy matters**: Countries with similar prosperity levels can have very different per capita emissions depending on their energy mix — France and the UK emit far less per capita than Germany or the US.
    68	- **Mixed 2024 signals**: While many developed nations reduced emissions in 2024, increases in parts of Asia, the Middle East, and Africa offset some of these gains.

     2	name: ppt-master
     3	description: >
     4	  AI-driven multi-format SVG content generation system. Converts source documents
     5	  (PDF/DOCX/URL/Markdown) into high-quality SVG pages and exports to PPTX through
     6	  multi-role collaboration. Use when user asks to "create PPT", "make presentation",
     7	  "生成PPT", "做PPT", "制作演示文稿", or mentions "ppt-master".
     8	---
     9	
    10	# PPT Master Skill
    11	
    12	> AI-driven multi-format SVG content generation system. Converts source documents into high-quality SVG pages through multi-role collaboration and exports to PPTX.
    13	
    14	**Core Pipeline**: `Source Document → Create Project → Template Option → Strategist → [Image_Generator] → Executor → Post-processing → Export`
    15	
    16	> [!CAUTION]
    17	> ## 🚨 Global Execution Discipline (MANDATORY)
    18	>
    19	> **This workflow is a strict serial pipeline. The following rules have the highest priority — violating any one of them constitutes execution failure:**
    20	>
    21	> 1. **SERIAL EXECUTION** — Steps MUST be executed in order; the output of each step is the input for the next. Non-BLOCKING adjacent steps may proceed continuously once prerequisites are met, without waiting for the user to say "continue"
    22	> 2. **BLOCKING = CONFIRMATION POINT** — Steps marked ⛔ BLOCKING are confirmation checkpoints. If a user is present, pause and wait for confirmation. If no user is available (e.g. automated / non-interactive mode), the AI should make professional recommendations based on the source material and proceed automatically
    23	> 3. **NO CROSS-PHASE BUNDLING** — Cross-phase bundling is FORBIDDEN. (Note: the Eight Confirmations in Step 4 are ⛔ BLOCKING — the AI should present recommendations and seek user confirmation when possible. Once confirmed (or auto-decided in non-interactive mode), all subsequent non-BLOCKING steps — design spec output, SVG generation, speaker notes, and post-processing — may proceed automatically without further confirmation)
    24	> 4. **GATE BEFORE ENTRY** — Each Step has prerequisites (🚧 GATE) listed at the top; these MUST be verified before starting that Step
    25	> 5. **NO SPECULATIVE EXECUTION** — "Pre-preparing" content for subsequent Steps is FORBIDDEN (e.g., writing SVG code during the Strategist phase)
    26	> 6. **NO SUB-AGENT SVG GENERATION** — Executor Step 6 SVG generation is context-dependent and MUST be completed by the current main agent end-to-end. Delegating page SVG generation to sub-agents is FORBIDDEN
    27	> 7. **SEQUENTIAL PAGE GENERATION ONLY** — In Executor Step 6, after the global design context is confirmed, SVG pages MUST be generated sequentially page by page in one continuous pass. Grouped page batches (for example, 5 pages at a time) are FORBIDDEN
    28	
    29	> [!IMPORTANT]
    30	> ## 🌐 Language & Communication Rule
    31	>
    32	> - **Response language**: Always match the language of the user's input and provided source materials. For example, if the user asks in Chinese, respond in Chinese; if the source material is in English, respond in English.
    33	> - **Explicit override**: If the user explicitly requests a specific language (e.g., "请用英文回答" or "Reply in Chinese"), use that language instead.
    34	> - **Template format**: The `design_spec.md` file MUST always follow its original English template structure (section headings, field names), regardless of the conversation language. Content values within the template may be in the user's language.
    35	
    36	> [!IMPORTANT]
    37	> ## 🔌 Compatibility With Generic Coding Skills
    38	>
    39	> - `ppt-master` is a repository-specific workflow skill, not a general application scaffold
    40	> - Do NOT create or require `.worktrees/`, `tests/`, branch workflows, or other generic engineering structure by default
    41	> - If another generic coding skill suggests repository conventions that conflict with this workflow, follow this skill first unless the user explicitly asks otherwise
    42	
    43	## Main Pipeline Scripts
    44	
    45	| Script | Purpose |
    46	|--------|---------|
    47	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/pdf_to_md.py` | PDF to Markdown |
    48	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/doc_to_md.py` | Documents to Markdown via Pandoc (DOCX, EPUB, HTML, LaTeX, RST, etc.) |
    49	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/web_to_md.py` | Web page to Markdown |
    50	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/web_to_md.cjs` | WeChat / high-security sites to Markdown |
    51	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/project_manager.py` | Project init / validate / manage |
    52	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/analyze_images.py` | Image analysis |
    53	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/image_gen.py` | AI image generation (multi-provider) |
    54	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/svg_quality_checker.py` | SVG quality check |
    55	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/total_md_split.py` | Speaker notes splitting |
    56	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/finalize_svg.py` | SVG post-processing (unified entry) |
    57	| `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/svg_to_pptx.py` | Export to PPTX |
    58	
    59	For complete tool documentation, see `${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/README.md`.
    60	
    61	## Template Index
    62	
    63	| Index | Path | Purpose |
    64	|-------|------|---------|
    65	| Layout templates | `${SKILL_DIR}/templates/layouts/layouts_index.json` | Query available page layout templates |
    66	| Chart templates | `${SKILL_DIR}/templates/charts/charts_index.json` | Query available chart SVG templates |
    67	| Icon library | `${SKILL_DIR}/templates/icons/icons_index.json` | Query available icon names and categories |
    68	
    69	## Standalone Workflows
    70	
    71	| Workflow | Path | Purpose |
    72	|----------|------|---------|
    73	| `create-template` | `workflows/create-template.md` | Standalone template creation workflow |
    74	
    75	---
    76	
    77	## Workflow
    78	
    79	### Step 1: Source Content Processing
    80	
    81	🚧 **GATE**: User has provided source material (PDF / DOCX / EPUB / URL / Markdown file / text description / conversation content — any form is acceptable).
    82	
    83	When the user provides non-Markdown content, convert immediately:
    84	
    85	| User Provides | Command |
    86	|---------------|---------|
    87	| PDF file | `python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/pdf_to_md.py <file>` |
    88	| DOCX / Word / Office document | `python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/doc_to_md.py <file>` |
    89	| EPUB / HTML / LaTeX / RST / other | `python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/doc_to_md.py <file>` |
    90	| Web link | `python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/web_to_md.py <URL>` |
    91	| WeChat / high-security site | `node ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/web_to_md.cjs <URL>` |
    92	| Markdown | Read directly |
    93	
    94	**✅ Checkpoint — Confirm source content is ready, proceed to Step 2.**
    95	
    96	---
    97	
    98	### Step 2: Project Initialization
    99	
   100	🚧 **GATE**: Step 1 complete; source content is ready (Markdown file, user-provided text, or requirements described in conversation are all valid).
   101	
   102	```bash
   103	python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/project_manager.py init <project_name> --format <format>
   104	```
   105	
   106	Format options: `ppt169` (default), `ppt43`, `xhs`, `story`, etc. For the full format list, see `references/canvas-formats.md`.
   107	
   108	Import source content (choose based on the situation):
   109	
   110	| Situation | Action |
   111	|-----------|--------|
   112	| Has source files (PDF/MD/etc.) | `python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/project_manager.py import-sources <project_path> <source_files...> --move` |
   113	| User provided text directly in conversation | No import needed — content is already in conversation context; subsequent steps can reference it directly |
   114	
   115	> ⚠️ **MUST use `--move`**: All source files (original PDF / MD / images) MUST be **moved** (not copied) into `sources/` for archiving.
   116	> - Markdown files generated in Step 1, original PDFs, original MDs — **all** must be moved into the project via `import-sources --move`
   117	> - Intermediate artifacts (e.g., `_files/` directories) are handled automatically by `import-sources`
   118	> - After execution, source files no longer exist at their original location
   119	
   120	**✅ Checkpoint — Confirm project structure created successfully, `sources/` contains all source files, converted materials are ready. Proceed to Step 3.**
   121	
   122	---
   123	
   124	### Step 3: Template Selection
   125	
   126	🚧 **GATE**: Step 2 complete; project directory structure is ready.
   127	
   128	⛔ **BLOCKING**: If the user has not yet clearly expressed whether to use a template, present options and seek user input. If no user is available, choose the most appropriate template based on content topic and tone, or choose free-design. If the user has previously stated "no template" or specified a particular template, skip this prompt and proceed directly.
   129	
   130	**Template recommendation flow** (only when the user has NOT yet decided):
   131	Query `${SKILL_DIR}/templates/layouts/layouts_index.json` to list available templates and their style descriptions.
   132	**When presenting options, you MUST provide a professional recommendation based on the current PPT topic and content** (recommend a specific template or free design, with reasoning), then ask the user:
   133	
   134	> 💡 **AI Recommendation**: Based on your content topic (brief summary), I recommend **[specific template / free design]** because...
   135	>
   136	> Which approach would you prefer?
   137	> **A) Use an existing template** (please specify template name or style preference)
   138	> **B) No template** — free design
   139	
   140	After the user confirms option A, copy template files to the project directory:
   141	```bash
   142	cp ${SKILL_DIR}/templates/layouts/<template_name>/*.svg <project_path>/templates/
   143	cp ${SKILL_DIR}/templates/layouts/<template_name>/design_spec.md <project_path>/templates/
   144	cp ${SKILL_DIR}/templates/layouts/<template_name>/*.png <project_path>/images/ 2>/dev/null || true
   145	cp ${SKILL_DIR}/templates/layouts/<template_name>/*.jpg <project_path>/images/ 2>/dev/null || true
   146	```
   147	
   148	After the user confirms option B, proceed directly to Step 4.
   149	
   150	> To create a new global template, read `workflows/create-template.md`
   151	
   152	**✅ Checkpoint — User has responded with template selection, template files copied (if option A). Proceed to Step 4.**
   153	
   154	---
   155	
   156	### Step 4: Strategist Phase (MANDATORY — cannot be skipped)
   157	
   158	🚧 **GATE**: Step 3 complete; user has confirmed template selection.
   159	
   160	First, read the role definition:
   161	```
   162	Read references/strategist.md
   163	```
   164	
   165	**Must complete the Eight Confirmations** (refer to `templates/design_spec_reference.md` for the template structure):
   166	
   167	⛔ **BLOCKING**: The Eight Confirmations should be presented to the user as a bundled set of recommendations. If a user is available, wait for confirmation or modification. If no user is available, apply professional defaults: read canvas/page-count/audience/style from the task input, and choose color/icon/typography/image settings based on content and tone. Once confirmed (or auto-decided), all subsequent script execution and slide generation should proceed fully automatically.
   168	
   169	1. Canvas format
   170	2. Page count range
   171	3. Target audience
   172	4. Style objective
   173	5. Color scheme
   174	6. Icon usage approach
   175	7. Typography plan
   176	8. Image usage approach
   177	
   178	If the user has provided images, run the analysis script **before outputting the design spec** (do NOT directly read/open image files — use the script output only):
   179	```bash
   180	python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/analyze_images.py <project_path>/images
   181	```
   182	
   183	> ⚠️ **Image handling rule**: The AI must NEVER directly read, open, or view image files (`.jpg`, `.png`, etc.). All image information must come from the `analyze_images.py` script output or the Design Specification's Image Resource List.
   184	
   185	**Output**: `<project_path>/design_spec.md`
   186	
   187	**✅ Checkpoint — Phase deliverables complete, auto-proceed to next step**:
   188	```markdown
   189	## ✅ Strategist Phase Complete
   190	- [x] Eight Confirmations completed (user confirmed)
   191	- [x] Design Specification & Content Outline generated
   192	- [ ] **Next**: Auto-proceed to [Image_Generator / Executor] phase
   193	```
   194	
   195	---
   196	
   197	### Step 5: Image_Generator Phase (Conditional)
   198	
   199	🚧 **GATE**: Step 4 complete; Design Specification & Content Outline generated and user confirmed.
   200	
   201	> **Trigger condition**: Image approach includes "AI generation". If not triggered, skip directly to Step 6 (Step 6 GATE must still be satisfied).
   202	
   203	Read `references/image-generator.md`
   204	
   205	1. Extract all images with status "pending generation" from the design spec
   206	2. Generate prompt document → `<project_path>/images/image_prompts.md`
   207	3. Generate images (CLI tool recommended):
   208	   ```bash
   209	   python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/image_gen.py "prompt" --aspect_ratio 16:9 --image_size 1K -o <project_path>/images
   210	   ```
   211	
   212	**✅ Checkpoint — Confirm all images are ready, proceed to Step 6**:
   213	```markdown
   214	## ✅ Image_Generator Phase Complete
   215	- [x] Prompt document created
   216	- [x] All images saved to images/
   217	```
   218	
   219	---
   220	
   221	### Step 6: Executor Phase
   222	
   223	🚧 **GATE**: Step 4 (and Step 5 if triggered) complete; all prerequisite deliverables are ready.
   224	
   225	Read the role definition based on the selected style:
   226	```
   227	Read references/executor-base.md          # REQUIRED: common guidelines
   228	Read references/executor-general.md       # General flexible style
   229	Read references/executor-consultant.md    # Consulting style
   230	Read references/executor-consultant-top.md # Top consulting style (MBB level)
   231	```
   232	
   233	> Only need to read executor-base + one style file.
   234	
   235	**Design Parameter Confirmation (Mandatory)**: Before generating the first SVG, the Executor MUST review and output key design parameters from the Design Specification (canvas dimensions, color scheme, font plan, body font size) to ensure spec adherence. See executor-base.md Section 2 for details.
   236	
   237	> ⚠️ **Main-agent only rule**: SVG generation in Step 6 MUST remain with the current main agent because page design depends on full upstream context (source content, design spec, template mapping, image decisions, and cross-page consistency). Do NOT delegate any slide SVG generation to sub-agents.
   238	> ⚠️ **Generation rhythm rule**: After confirming the global design parameters, the Executor MUST generate pages sequentially, one page at a time, while staying in the same continuous main-agent context. Do NOT split Step 6 into grouped page batches such as 5 pages per batch.
   239	
   240	**Visual Construction Phase**:
   241	- Generate SVG pages sequentially, one page at a time, in one continuous pass → `<project_path>/svg_output/`
   242	
   243	**Logic Construction Phase**:
   244	- Generate speaker notes → `<project_path>/notes/total.md`
   245	
   246	**✅ Checkpoint — Confirm all SVGs and notes are fully generated. Proceed directly to Step 7 post-processing**:
   247	```markdown
   248	## ✅ Executor Phase Complete
   249	- [x] All SVGs generated to svg_output/
   250	- [x] Speaker notes generated at notes/total.md
   251	```
   252	
   253	---
   254	
   255	### Step 7: Post-processing & Export
   256	
   257	🚧 **GATE**: Step 6 complete; all SVGs generated to `svg_output/`; speaker notes `notes/total.md` generated.
   258	
   259	> ⚠️ The following three sub-steps MUST be **executed individually one at a time**. Each command must complete and be confirmed successful before running the next.
   260	> ❌ **NEVER** put all three commands in a single code block or single shell invocation.
   261	
   262	**Step 7.1** — Split speaker notes:
   263	```bash
   264	python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/total_md_split.py <project_path>
   265	```
   266	
   267	**Step 7.2** — SVG post-processing (icon embedding / image crop & embed / text flattening / rounded rect to path):
   268	```bash
   269	python3 ${SKILL_DIR}/scripts/finalize_svg.py <project_path>
   270	```
   271	
   272	**Step 7.3** — Export PPTX (embeds speaker notes by default):
   273	```bash

1	# Role: Strategist
     2	
     3	## Core Mission
     4	
     5	As a top-tier AI presentation strategist, receive source documents, perform content analysis and design planning, and output the **Design Specification & Content Outline** (hereafter `design_spec`).
     6	
     7	## Pipeline Context
     8	
     9	| Previous Step | Current | Next Step |
    10	|--------------|---------|-----------|
    11	| Project creation + Template option confirmed | **Strategist**: Eight Confirmations + Design Spec | Image_Generator or Executor |
    12	
    13	> See shared-standards.md for SVG technical constraints, PPT compatibility rules, canvas format table, and post-processing commands.
    14	
    15	---
    16	
    17	## 1. Eight Confirmations Process
    18	
    19	⛔ **BLOCKING**: Before starting analysis, reference `templates/design_spec_reference.md` and provide professional recommendations for the following eight items. If a user is available, present them as a bundled package and wait for confirmation or modifications. If no user is available, apply the recommendations directly and proceed.
    20	
    21	> **Execution discipline**: This is the last BLOCKING checkpoint in the pipeline (besides template selection). Once confirmed (or auto-decided in non-interactive mode), the AI must automatically complete the Design Specification & Content Outline and seamlessly proceed to subsequent image generation (if applicable), SVG generation, and post-processing — no additional questions or pauses in between.
    22	
    23	### a. Canvas Format Confirmation
    24	
    25	Recommend format based on scenario (see canvas format quick reference in shared-standards.md).
    26	
    27	### b. Page Count Confirmation
    28	
    29	Provide specific page count recommendation based on source document content volume.
    30	
    31	### c. Key Information Confirmation
    32	
    33	Confirm target audience, usage occasion, and core message; provide initial assessment based on document nature.
    34	
    35	### d. Style Objective Confirmation
    36	
    37	| Style | Core Focus | Target Audience | One-line Description |
    38	|-------|-----------|----------------|---------------------|
    39	| **A) General Versatile** | Visual impact first | Public / clients / trainees | "Catch the eye at a glance" |
    40	| **B) General Consulting** | Data clarity first | Teams / management | "Let data speak" |
    41	| **C) Top Consulting** | Logical persuasion first | Executives / board | "Lead with conclusions" |
    42	
    43	**Style selection decision tree**:
    44	
    45	```
    46	Content characteristics?
    47	  ├── Heavy imagery / promotional ──→ A) General Versatile
    48	  ├── Data analysis / progress report ──→ B) General Consulting
    49	  └── Strategic decisions / persuading executives ──→ C) Top Consulting
    50	
    51	Audience?
    52	  ├── Public / clients / trainees ────→ A) General Versatile
    53	  ├── Teams / management ────────────→ B) General Consulting
    54	  └── Executives / board / investors → C) Top Consulting
    55	```
    56	
    57	### e. Color Scheme Recommendation
    58	
    59	Proactively provide a color scheme (HEX values) based on content characteristics and industry.
    60	
    61	**Industry color quick reference** (full 14-industry list in `scripts/config.py` under `INDUSTRY_COLORS`):
    62	
    63	| Industry | Primary Color | Characteristics |
    64	|----------|--------------|-----------------|
    65	| Finance / Business | `#003366` Navy Blue | Stable, trustworthy |
    66	| Technology / Internet | `#1565C0` Bright Blue | Innovative, energetic |
    67	| Healthcare / Health | `#00796B` Teal Green | Professional, reassuring |
    68	| Government / Public Sector | `#C41E3A` Red | Authoritative, dignified |
    69	
    70	**Color rules**: 60-30-10 rule (primary 60%, secondary 30%, accent 10%); text contrast ratio >= 4.5:1; no more than 4 colors per page.
    71	
    72	### f. Icon Usage Confirmation
    73	
    74	| Option | Approach | Suitable Scenarios |
    75	|--------|----------|-------------------|
    76	| **A** | Emoji | Casual, playful, social media |
    77	| **B** | AI-generated | Custom style needed |
    78	| **C** | Built-in icon library | Professional scenarios (recommended) |
    79	| **D** | Custom icons | Has brand assets |
    80	
    81	Built-in library contains 640+ icons; see `templates/icons/README.md`.
    82	
    83	> **Mandatory rules when choosing C**:
    84	> 1. Consult `templates/icons/icons_index.json` to verify icon existence
    85	> 2. Icon names are single names (e.g., `factory`), no path prefixes
    86	> 3. Using names not in the index is FORBIDDEN

    88	>
    89	> **Quick lookup**: By category → `icons_index.json` `categories`; by semantics → `quickLookup`; full list → `templates/icons/FULL_INDEX.md`
    90	
    91	### g. Typography Plan Confirmation (Font + Size)
    92	
    93	#### Font Presets
    94	
    95	| Scenario | Preset | Title | Body | Emphasis |

    97	| Modern business, tech | P1 | Microsoft YaHei / Arial | Microsoft YaHei / Calibri | SimHei |
    98	| Government documents, reports | P2 | SimHei | SimSun / Times | SimSun |
    99	| Culture, arts, humanities | P3 | KaiTi / Georgia | Microsoft YaHei | SimHei |
   100	| Traditional, conservative | P4 | SimSun | Microsoft YaHei / Arial | SimSun |
   101	| English-primary | P5 | Arial / Impact | Calibri / Georgia | Arial Black |

   104	
   105	Selection principle: Font size is based on **content density**, not design style.
   106

     7	## 1. SVG Banned Features Blacklist
     8	
     9	The following features are **absolutely forbidden** when generating SVGs — PPT export will break if any are used:
    10	
    11	| Banned Feature | Description |
    12	|----------------|-------------|
    13	| `clipPath` | Clipping paths |
    14	| `mask` | Masks |
    15	| `<style>` | Embedded stylesheets |
    16	| `class` | CSS selector attributes (`id` inside `<defs>` is a legitimate reference and is NOT banned) |
    17	| External CSS | External stylesheet links |
    18	| `<foreignObject>` | Embedded external content |
    19	| `<symbol>` + `<use>` | Symbol reference reuse |
    20	| `textPath` | Text along a path |
    21	| `@font-face` | Custom font declarations |
    22	| `<animate*>` / `<set>` | SVG animations |
    23	| `<script>` / event attributes | Scripts and interactivity |
    24	| `marker` / `marker-end` | Line endpoint markers |
    25	| `<iframe>` | Embedded frames |
    26	
    27	---
    28	
    29	## 2. PPT Compatibility Alternatives
    30	
    31	| Banned Syntax | Correct Alternative |
    32	|---------------|---------------------|
    33	| `fill="rgba(255,255,255,0.1)"` | `fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.1"` |
    34	| `<g opacity="0.2">...</g>` | Set `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity` on each child element individually |
    35	| `<image opacity="0.3"/>` | Overlay a `<rect fill="background-color" opacity="0.7"/>` mask layer after the image |
    36	| `marker-end` arrows | Draw triangle arrows with `<polygon>` |
    37	
    38	**Mnemonic**: PPT does not recognize rgba, group opacity, image opacity, or markers.

    70	## 4. Basic SVG Rules
    71	
    72	- **viewBox** must match the canvas dimensions (`width`/`height` must match `viewBox`)
    73	- **Background**: Use `<rect>` to define the page background color
    74	- **Line breaks**: Use `<tspan>` for manual line breaks; `<foreignObject>` is FORBIDDEN
    75	- **Fonts**: Use system fonts only (Microsoft YaHei, Arial, Calibri, etc.); `@font-face` is FORBIDDEN
    76	- **Styles**: Use inline styles only (`fill="..."` `font-size="..."`); `<style>` / `class` are FORBIDDEN (`id` inside `<defs>` is legitimate)
    77	- **Colors**: Use HEX values; for transparency use `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity`
    78	- **Image references**: `<image href="../images/xxx.png" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"/>`
    79	- **Icon placeholders**: `<use data-icon="icon-name" x="" y="" width="48" height="48" fill="#HEX"/>` (auto-embedded during post-processing)

   107	
   108	## 6. Shadow & Overlay Techniques
   109	
   110	> `<mask>` elements and `<image opacity="...">` are banned. Always use stacked `<rect>` or gradient overlays instead (see §2).
   111	
   112	### Shadow
   113	
   114	#### Filter Soft Shadow — Recommended
   115	
   116	Best for: cards, floating panels, elevated elements. `svg_to_shapes.py` automatically converts `feGaussianBlur` + `feOffset` into native PPTX `<a:outerShdw>`.
   117	
   118	```xml
   119	<defs>
   120	  <filter id="softShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   121	    <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="8"/>
   122	    <feOffset dx="0" dy="4" result="offsetBlur"/>
   123	    <feFlood flood-color="#000000" flood-opacity="0.08" result="shadowColor"/>
   124	    <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   125	    <feMerge>
   126	      <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   127	      <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   128	    </feMerge>
   129	  </filter>
   130	</defs>
   131	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" filter="url(#softShadow)"/>
   132	```
   133	
   134	Recommended parameters:
   135	```
   136	stdDeviation:   6–10     (smaller = crisper, larger = softer)
   137	flood-opacity:  0.06–0.12  (keep low for a premium feel)
   138	dy:             3–6      (vertical > horizontal for natural top-light)
   139	dx:             0–2
   140	```
   141	
   142	#### Colored Shadow
   143	
   144	Best for: accent buttons, brand-colored cards. Use the element's own color family instead of black.
   145	
   146	```xml
   147	<filter id="colorShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   148	  <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="10"/>
   149	  <feOffset dx="0" dy="6" result="offsetBlur"/>
   150	  <feFlood flood-color="#1A73E8" flood-opacity="0.20" result="shadowColor"/>
   151	  <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   152	  <feMerge>
   153	    <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   154	    <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   155	  </feMerge>
   156	</filter>
   157	```
   158	
   159	Replace `flood-color` with the element's brand color; keep `flood-opacity` between 0.12–0.20.
   160	
   161	#### Layered Rect Shadow — High-Compatibility Fallback
   162	
   163	Best for: maximum compatibility with older PowerPoint versions. Stack 2–3 semi-transparent rectangles behind the main card:
   164	
   165	```xml
   166	<!-- Shadow layers (back to front, largest offset first) -->
   167	<rect x="68" y="72" width="400" height="240" rx="16" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.03"/>
   168	<rect x="65" y="69" width="400" height="240" rx="14" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.05"/>
   169	<rect x="62" y="66" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#1A73E8" fill-opacity="0.04"/>
   170	<!-- Main card -->
   171	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
   172	```
   173	
   174	### Image Overlay
   175	
   176	#### Linear Gradient Overlay — Most Common
   177	
   178	Best for: image+text pages. Gradient direction should match text position (text on left → gradient darkens toward left).
   179	
   180	```xml
   181	<image href="..." x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"/>
   182	<defs>
   183	  <linearGradient id="imgOverlay" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
   184	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.85"/>
   185	    <stop offset="55%"  stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.30"/>
   186	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0"/>
   187	  </linearGradient>
   188	</defs>
   189	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#imgOverlay)"/>
   190	```
   191	
   192	#### Bottom Gradient Bar
   193	
   194	Best for: cover slides and full-image pages with bottom title.
   195	
   196	```xml
   197	<defs>
   198	  <linearGradient id="bottomBar" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
   199	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0"/>
   200	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0.72"/>
   201	  </linearGradient>
   202	</defs>
   203	<rect x="0" y="380" width="1280" height="340" fill="url(#bottomBar)"/>
   204	```
   205	
   206	#### Radial Gradient Overlay — Vignette Effect
   207	
   208	Best for: full-screen atmosphere slides; draws attention to the center.
   209	
   210	```xml
   211	<defs>
   212	  <radialGradient id="vignette" cx="50%" cy="50%" r="70%">
   213	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0"/>
   214	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#000000" stop-opacity="0.58"/>
   215	  </radialGradient>
   216	</defs>
   217	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#vignette)"/>
   218	```
   219	
   220	#### Brand Color Overlay
   221	
   222	Best for: slides needing strong visual brand identity.
   223	
   224	```xml
   225	<defs>
   226	  <linearGradient id="brandOverlay" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
   227	    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#005587" stop-opacity="0.80"/>
   228	    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#005587" stop-opacity="0.10"/>
   229	  </linearGradient>
   230	</defs>
   231	<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#brandOverlay)"/>
   232	```
   233	
   234	### Quick-Reference Table
   235	
   236	| Scenario | Recommended Technique | Avoid |
   237	|----------|-----------------------|-------|
   238	| Card / panel shadow | Filter soft shadow (`flood-opacity` ≤ 0.12) | Hard black shadow |
   239	| Accent / CTA button | Colored shadow (same hue family) | Generic gray shadow |
   240	| Text over image | Linear gradient overlay (direction matches text side) | Uniform flat opacity over whole image |
   241	| Cover / full-image slide | Bottom gradient bar + brand color | Solid black overlay |
   242	| Atmosphere / hero slide | Radial vignette | Unprocessed raw image |
   243	| Max PPT compatibility needed | Layered rect shadow | Filter-based shadow |

# Global CO₂ Emissions - Design Spec

## I. Project Information

| Item | Value |
| ---- | ----- |
| **Project Name** | co2_emissions |
| **Canvas Format** | PPT 16:9 (1280×720) |
| **Page Count** | 9 |
| **Design Style** | Top Consulting (McKinsey-style) |
| **Target Audience** | Policy analysts, climate negotiators, sustainability researchers |
| **Use Case** | Executive briefing on global CO₂ emission trends, regional shifts, and per-capita inequalities |
| **Created Date** | 2026-04-27 |

---

## II. Canvas Specification

| Property | Value |
| -------- | ----- |
| **Format** | PPT 16:9 |
| **Dimensions** | 1280 × 720 px |
| **viewBox** | `0 0 1280 720` |
| **Margins** | Left/Right 60px, Top 60px, Bottom 40px |
| **Content Area** | x: 60–1220, y: 60–680 |

---

## III. Visual Theme

### Theme Style

- **Style**: Top Consulting — data-forward, analytical, accessible
- **Theme**: Light theme (white background + deep navy accent)
- **Tone**: Professional authority, climate-policy gravitas, data clarity

### Color Scheme

| Role | HEX | Purpose |
| ---- | --- | ------- |
| **Background** | `#FFFFFF` | Page background |
| **Secondary bg** | `#F4F6F8` | Card backgrounds, chart panels |
| **Primary** | `#0B3D4C` | Title decorations, header bar, key sections |
| **Accent** | `#2E8B8B` | Data highlights, key information, positive trends |
| **Secondary accent** | `#D4A843` | Amber emphasis, important callouts |
| **Body text** | `#1F2937` | Main body text |
| **Secondary text** | `#5D6D7E` | Captions, annotations, axis labels |
| **Tertiary text** | `#8B9DAE` | Supplementary info, footers |
| **Border/divider** | `#D5DDE5` | Card borders, divider lines |
| **Success/Decline** | `#2E7D6F` | Emission declines (positive) |
| **Warning/Rise** | `#C45B3A` | Emission increases (negative) |

### Gradient Scheme

```xml
<!-- Title accent gradient -->
<linearGradient id="titleGradient" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="100%">
  <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#0B3D4C"/>
  <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#2E8B8B"/>
</linearGradient>

<!-- Background decorative gradient -->
<radialGradient id="bgDecor" cx="85%" cy="15%" r="50%">
  <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#2E8B8B" stop-opacity="0.08"/>
  <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#2E8B8B" stop-opacity="0"/>
</radialGradient>
```

---

## IV. Typography System

### Font Plan

**Recommended preset**: P5 (English-primary)

| Role | Chinese | English | Fallback |
| ---- | ------- | ------- | -------- |
| **Title** | — | Arial | "Helvetica Neue", sans-serif |
| **Body** | — | Calibri | Georgia, serif |
| **Code** | — | Consolas | Monaco |
| **Emphasis** | — | Arial Black | Arial, sans-serif |

**Font stack**: `Arial, "Helvetica Neue", "Segoe UI", Calibri, sans-serif`

### Font Size Hierarchy

**Baseline**: Body font size = 18px (dense data content)

| Purpose | Ratio | Size | Weight |
| ------- | ----- | ---- | ------ |
| Cover title | 2.5–3x | 48px | Bold |
| Page title | 1.5–2x | 32px | Bold |
| Subtitle | 1.2–1.5x | 22px | SemiBold |
| **Body content** | **1x** | **18px** | Regular |
| Annotation | 0.75x | 14px | Regular |
| Page number/date | 0.55x | 11px | Regular |
| Data highlight | 2x | 36px | Bold |

---

## V. Layout Principles

### Page Structure

- **Header area**: y=0, h=4px — Primary color horizontal bar
- **Title area**: y=40, h=60px — Page title (left-aligned, bold)
- **Content area**: y=110, h=530px — Main content area
- **Footer area**: y=680, h=40px — Page number + data source attribution

### Common Layout Modes

| Mode | Suitable Scenarios |
| ---- | ----------------- |
| **Single column centered** | Cover, key takeaways |
| **Left-right split (5:5)** | Comparative analysis |
| **Top-bottom split** | Chart + annotation |
| **Card grid (2–3 columns)** | KPI overviews, feature lists |

### Spacing Specification

| Element | Recommended Range | Current Project |
| ------- | ---------------- | --------------- |
| Card gap | 20–32px | 24px |
| Content block gap | 24–40px | 32px |
| Card padding | 20–32px | 24px |
| Card border radius | 8–12px | 8px |
| Icon-text gap | 8–12px | 10px |

---

## VI. Icon Usage Specification

### Source

- **Built-in icon library**: `templates/icons/` (640+ icons)
- **Usage method**: Placeholder format `{{icon:category/icon-name}}`

### Recommended Icon List

| Purpose | Icon Path | Page |
| ------- | --------- | ---- |
| Globe/World | `{{icon:globe/world}}` | Slide 01 |
| Factory/Industry | `{{icon:industry/factory}}` | Slide 02 |
| Chart trending up | `{{icon:chart/trending-up}}` | Slide 02 |
| Map/Location | `{{icon:map/location}}` | Slide 03 |
| Users/People | `{{icon:users/users}}` | Slide 05 |
| Scale/Balance | `{{icon:legal/scale}}` | Slide 09 |
| Lightbulb/Energy | `{{icon:energy/lightbulb}}` | Slide 08 |
| Alert/Warning | `{{icon:alert/warning}}` | Slide 07 |

---

## VII. Chart Reference List

| Chart Type | Reference Template | Used In | Purpose |
| ---------- | ------------------ | ------- | ------- |
| area_chart | `templates/charts/area_chart.svg` | Slide 02 | Global emission trajectory 1750–2024 |
| stacked_area_chart | `templates/charts/stacked_area_chart.svg` | Slide 03 | Regional share shift over time |
| treemap_chart | `templates/charts/treemap_chart.svg` | Slide 04 | Country-level share comparison |
| horizontal_bar_chart | `templates/charts/horizontal_bar_chart.svg` | Slide 05 | Per capita emission ranking |
| horizontal_bar_chart | `templates/charts/horizontal_bar_chart.svg` | Slide 06 | Per capita snapshot comparison |
| bar_chart | `templates/charts/bar_chart.svg` | Slide 07 | 2024 annual change diverging bars |
| grouped_bar_chart | `templates/charts/grouped_bar_chart.svg` | Slide 08 | Energy mix comparison |

---

## VIII. Image Resource List

No AI-generated images required. All visuals are data-driven charts and geometric decorations.

| Filename | Dimensions | Ratio | Purpose | Type | Status | Generation Description |
| -------- | --------- | ----- | ------- | ---- | ------ | --------------------- |
| — | — | — | — | — | — | No images needed |

---

## IX. Content Outline

### Part 1: Opening & Global Trajectory

#### Slide 01 — Cover
- **Layout**: Single column centered (cover)
- **Title**: Global CO₂ Emissions: Who Emits, How Much, and What's Changing
- **Subtitle**: Fossil fuels & industry, 1750–2024
- **Info**: Data: Global Carbon Budget 2025 via Our World in Data | Audience: Policy analysts, climate negotiators, sustainability researchers
- **Chart**: None

#### Slide 02 — Global Emissions Growth
- **Layout**: Top-bottom split (chart dominant)
- **Title**: Global CO₂ Emissions Grew from 6 Bt in 1950 to Over 35 Bt Today
- **Chart**: area_chart
- **Content**:
  - Pre-industrial: negligible emissions
  - 1950: ~6 Bt/year
  - 1990: ~20 Bt/year (nearly quadrupled)
  - 2024: >35 Bt/year
  - Growth has slowed but no peak yet
  - Fossil fuels dominate; land-use change declined slightly

### Part 2: Regional & Country Shifts

#### Slide 03 — Regional Share Shift
- **Layout**: Top-bottom split
- **Title**: Europe and the US Fell from 90% of Emissions in 1900 to Under One-Third Today
- **Chart**: stacked_area_chart
- **Content**:
  - 1900: Europe + US >90%
  - 1950: Europe + US >85%
  - Today: Europe + US <33%
  - Asia (led by China) now ~50% of global emissions

#### Slide 04 — China Dominates Share
- **Layout**: Left-right split (chart + key stats)
- **Title**: China Now Emits More Than One-Quarter of Global CO₂
- **Chart**: treemap_chart (or bar chart fallback)
- **Content**:
  - China ~31% — Rising, growth slowing
  - United States ~13% — Declining
  - India ~8% — Rising
  - EU-27 ~6% — Declining
  - Russia ~5% — Roughly stable
  - Africa ~3–4% — Slowly rising
  - South America ~3–4% — Roughly stable
  - Int'l aviation & shipping ~3% — Rising

### Part 3: Per Capita Inequality

#### Slide 05 — Per Capita Inequality
- **Layout**: Left-right split (chart + annotation)
- **Title**: Per Capita Emissions Range from 0.1 t in Chad to ~14 t in the US and Canada
- **Chart**: horizontal_bar_chart
- **Content**:
  - US ~14 t, Canada ~14 t
  - China ~9 t, South Africa ~7 t
  - EU-27 ~6 t, World avg ~4.5 t
  - UK ~4 t, India ~2 t
  - Kenya ~0.4 t, Chad/Niger ~0.1 t
  - Gap: ~150x between lowest and highest large-country emitters
  - An American emits in under 2 days what a Nigerien emits in a year

#### Slide 06 — Per Capita Trends Over Time
- **Layout**: Top-bottom split (chart + insight callout)
- **Title**: Per Capita Emissions Vary Widely: ~14 t in the US vs. ~9 t in China and ~2 t in India
- **Chart**: horizontal_bar_chart
- **Content**:
  - US ~14 t, Canada ~14 t
  - China ~9 t (largest total emitter, but per capita below US)
  - South Africa ~7 t, EU-27 ~6 t
  - World average ~4.5 t, UK ~4 t
  - India ~2 t (very low despite large population)
  - Kenya ~0.4 t, Chad/Niger ~0.1 t
  - China's per capita remains below the US despite being largest total emitter

### Part 4: 2024 Trends & Energy Policy

#### Slide 07 — Annual Change 2024
- **Layout**: Left-right split (map placeholder + key findings)
- **Title**: 2024 Snapshot: Many Western Nations Cut Emissions While Parts of Asia and Africa Grew
- **Chart**: bar_chart (diverging style)
- **Content**:
  - US, much of EU, UK: declines (blue)
  - Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, several African nations: increases (red/orange)
  - Central Asia (Turkmenistan/Uzbekistan): increases >10%
  - Mixed picture — gains in West offset by rises elsewhere

#### Slide 08 — Energy Mix Matters
- **Layout**: Left-right split (comparison bars + text)
- **Title**: Energy Mix Explains Why France and the UK Emit Far Less Per Capita Than Germany or the US
- **Chart**: grouped_bar_chart
- **Content**:
  - US ~14 t, UK ~4 t, EU-27 ~6 t
  - France, UK, Portugal: lower per capita due to nuclear + renewables
  - Germany, Netherlands, US: higher per capita due to fossil fuel dependence
  - Similar prosperity levels, very different emissions — energy policy matters

### Part 5: Conclusion

#### Slide 09 — Key Takeaways
- **Layout**: Single column centered (bullet list)
- **Title**: Key Takeaways: Responsibility Is Shared but Unequal
- **Chart**: None
- **Content**:
  1. Global emissions exceed 35 Bt/yr and haven't peaked despite slowing growth
  2. China is the largest annual emitter but per capita still below the US
  3. Historical responsibility is dominated by Europe and the US (>90% in 1900)
  4. Per capita gaps of 150x persist between richest and poorest nations
  5. Energy policy and technology choices can decouple prosperity from emissions

---

## X. Speaker Notes Requirements

- **File naming**: Match SVG names (`01_cover.svg` → `notes/01_cover.md`)
- **Total duration**: ~20 minutes (2–2.5 min per slide)
- **Notes style**: Formal, data-driven, conclusion-first
- **Presentation purpose**: Inform and persuade — equip policy audience with clear, evidence-based understanding of emission distribution and responsibility

---

## XI. Technical Constraints Reminder

### SVG Generation Must Follow:

1. viewBox: `0 0 1280 720`
2. Background uses `<rect>` elements
3. Text wrapping uses `<tspan>` (`<foreignObject>` FORBIDDEN)
4. Transparency uses `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity`; `rgba()` FORBIDDEN
5. FORBIDDEN: `clipPath`, `mask`, `<style>`, `class`, `foreignObject`
6. FORBIDDEN: `textPath`, `animate*`, `script`, `marker`/`marker-end`
7. Arrows use `<polygon>` triangles instead of `<marker>`

### PPT Compatibility Rules:

- `<g opacity="...">` FORBIDDEN (group opacity); set on each child element individually
- Image transparency uses overlay mask layer (`<rect fill="bg-color" opacity="0.x"/>`)
- Inline styles only; external CSS and `@font-face` FORBIDDEN

---

## XII. Design Checklist

### Pre-generation

- [x] Content fits page capacity
- [x] Layout mode selected correctly
- [x] Colors used semantically

### Post-generation

- [ ] viewBox = `0 0 1280 720`
- [ ] No `<foreignObject>` elements
- [ ] All text readable (>=14px)
- [ ] Content within safe area
- [ ] All elements aligned to grid
- [ ] Same elements maintain consistent style
- [ ] Colors conform to spec
- [ ] CRAP four-principle check passed

---

## XIII. Next Steps

1. ✅ Design spec complete
2. **Next step**: No AI images → Invoke **Executor** role to generate SVGs

1	# Executor Consultant Top — Top-tier Consulting Style (MBB Level)
     2	
     3	> Common guidelines: executor-base.md. Technical constraints: shared-standards.md.
     4	
     5	---
     6	
     7	## Role Definition
     8	
     9	An MBB-level (McKinsey / Bain / BCG) top-tier consulting style SVG design executor. Suitable for strategic planning, board presentations, investment roadshows, C-suite decision support, and other **premium consulting** scenarios. Core characteristics: data-driven insights, pyramid-structured narrative, extreme simplicity. Output targets C-level decision-makers.
    10	
    11	---
    12	
    13	## SCQA Framework (Narrative Structure)
    14	
    15	Every MBB-level presentation follows the SCQA narrative structure:
    16	
    17	| Element | Purpose | Typical Pages |
    18	|---------|---------|---------------|
    19	| **S - Situation** | Establish shared context | Cover / Pages 1-2 |
    20	| **C - Complication** | Introduce the problem / tension | Pages 2-3 |
    21	| **Q - Question** | The implicit or explicit question to solve | Transition page |
    22	| **A - Answer** | Core solution | All body pages |
    23	
    24	**Page sequencing**: Cover embodies S+C → Executive Summary answers Q → Chapters develop A → Closing revisits S
    25	
    26	**Title writing**:
    27	
    28	| SCQA Element | Weak Title | MBB-level Title |
    29	|-------------|------------|-----------------|
    30	| S | "Industry Background" | "Digital penetration surpasses 60%, industry enters deep waters" |
    31	| C | "Challenges Faced" | "Yet three structural contradictions constrain scaled deployment" |
    32	| Q | "Strategic Question" | "How to move from pilot to full deployment within 18 months?" |
    33	| A | "Solution" | "Three-phase path: Focus, Expand, Scale" |
    34	
    35	---
    36	
    37	## Data Contextualization (Never Present Data in Isolation)
    38	
    39	> **Golden Rule**: Never display a single data point in isolation. Every number needs context.
    40	
    41	| Method | Pattern | Visual Implementation |
    42	|--------|---------|----------------------|
    43	| **Time comparison** | "From X to Y" | Line chart + arrow annotating magnitude of change |
    44	| **Benchmark** | "X vs industry average Y" | Bar chart with gray dashed baseline |
    45	| **Competitive comparison** | "Us X vs Competitor Y" | Side-by-side bar chart, highlight own data |
    46	| **Target gap** | "Actual X / Target Y" | Progress bar + gap annotation |
    47	| **Ranking** | "Ranked #N of M" | Horizontal bar chart + highlight marker |
    48	
    49	**Data annotation three essentials**: Every data visualization must include (1) The value itself (large bold font) (2) Comparison reference (baseline / prior period / competitor) (3) Meaning interpretation ("So what?")
    50	
    51	```xml
    52	<text x="160" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-size="42" font-weight="bold" fill="#1E293B">97.3%</text>
    53	<text x="160" y="310" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#64748B">Industry avg 82% | Competitor A 89%</text>
    54	<text x="160" y="335" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#059669">Leading industry by 15.3 percentage points</text>
    55	```
    56	
    57	---
    58	
    59	## Pyramid Principle (Conclusion First)
    60	
    61	> Executives don't care about your *process* — they care about *results*.
    62	
    63	```
    64	         ┌─────────────────┐
    65	         │  Core Conclusion │   ← Page title / Takeaway
    66	         └────────┬────────┘
    67	      ┌───────────┼───────────┐
    68	  ┌───┴───┐  ┌───┴───┐  ┌───┴───┐
    69	  │ Arg 1 │  │ Arg 2 │  │ Arg 3 │   ← Key supporting points
    70	  └───────┘  └───────┘  └───────┘
    71	```
    72	
    73	| Level | Position | Font Size |
    74	|-------|----------|-----------|
    75	| Core conclusion | Takeaway Box | 16-18px bold |
    76	| Arguments | Content area body | 14-16px |
    77	| Supporting data | Charts / cards | 12-14px |
    78	
    79	**Contrast**: Title "Market Research Results" (wrong) → "Metaverse needs 5-10 years to reach scale" (right); Body "We researched... and found..." (wrong) → "Three arguments: (1)... (2)... (3)..." (right)
    80	
    81	---
    82	
    83	## MBB-level Layout Patterns
    84	
    85	### Content Page Standard Structure (1280x720)
    86	
    87	```
    88	┌──────────────────────────────────┐
    89	│ Gradient top bar (0,0 → 1280,6)  │
    90	├──────────────────────────────────┤
    91	│ Assertion title (x=40, y=50, 24px)│
    92	├──────────────────────────────────┤
    93	│ Takeaway Box (x=40, y=75,        │  ← Dark background + white text, one-sentence conclusion
    94	│   w=1200, h=45)                  │
    95	├──────────────────────────────────┤
    96	│ Content area (x=40, y=140,       │  ← Charts / data / analysis
    97	│   w=1200, h=520)                 │
    98	├──────────────────────────────────┤
    99	│ Source | CONFIDENTIAL | Page #    │  ← y=700, 10px
   100	└──────────────────────────────────┘
   101	```
   102	
   103	### Strategic Roadmap
   104	
   105	Three phases laid out horizontally, `<rect rx="8">` + title + action list, `<polygon>` arrows connecting:
   106	
   107	```
   108	Focus Core (0-6mo)  ──>  Expand Capability (6-12mo)  ──>  Scale Up (12-18mo)
   109	x=40,w=380              x=450,w=380                     x=860,w=380
   110	```
   111	
   112	### Benchmarking Matrix
   113	
   114	Horizontal table; own row highlighted in theme color, others in gray. Leading indicators marked green, lagging marked red. Use `<circle>` or `<rect>` to build score points.
   115	
   116	### Waterfall Chart (Change Attribution)
   117	
   118	Start → increase/decrease factors → End. Positive factors green bars, negative factors red bars, start/end points dark bars, cumulative line as dashed connector.
   119	
   120	---
   121	
   122	## Strategic Use of Color
   123	
   124	MBB-level color usage is extremely restrained — color serves information:
   125	
   126	| Purpose | Method |
   127	|---------|--------|
   128	| **Focus** | Target data in theme color, everything else gray |
   129	| **Reduce cognitive load** | Same series differentiated by opacity (`fill-opacity` 1.0/0.6/0.3) |
   130	| **Semantics** | Green = positive, Red = negative, Gray = baseline |
   131	| **Branding** | Gradient top bar / decorative lines in brand color |
   132	
   133	**Commandments**: No more than 3 primary colors; accent color used at most 2-3 places globally; data series use same-hue depth variations, not different colors; background white or very light gray.
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	## Chart vs Table Selection Matrix
   138	
   139	| Scenario | Recommended Form | Reason |
   140	|----------|-----------------|--------|
   141	| Comparing 2-7 categories | **Bar chart** | Visual comparison is intuitive |
   142	| Time trends | **Line chart** | Time series clarity |
   143	| Precise values / large rankings | **Table** | 50 data points in a bar chart would be chaotic |
   144	| Proportional composition | **Donut chart** | More modern than pie charts |
   145	| Two-dimensional positioning | **2x2 matrix** | Strategic quadrant analysis |
   146	| Change attribution | **Waterfall chart** | Factor decomposition |
   147	
   148	---
   149	
   150	## Speaker Notes Style
   151	
   152	### Narrative Tone
   153	
   154	Targeting **executives / decision-makers**. Pyramid structure — every sentence carries information. Composed, authoritative, and insightful tone.
   155	
   156	### Stage Direction Markers
   157	
   158	| Marker | Purpose | Example |
   159	|--------|---------|---------|
   160	| `[Pause]` | Silence after key insight, let executives absorb | "This means we are missing a billion-dollar market. [Pause]" |
   161	| `[Scan Room]` | Observe decision-makers' reactions, decide whether to elaborate | "[Scan Room] If there are questions, I can elaborate." |
   162	| `[Data]` | Conversational number delivery | "[Data] 63% → nearly two-thirds" |
   163	| `[Benchmark]` | Emphasize comparison baseline | "[Benchmark] Compared to the industry average of 12%, our 23% is nearly double" |
   164	| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Building on the strategic framework, let's drill into the implementation path." |
   165	
   166	### Notes Writing Guidelines
   167	
   168	- **Pyramid structure**: Conclusion → Arguments → Details
   169	- **Data contextualization**: Every number has a comparison reference
   170	- **Executive language**: "The strategic implication is...", "The core insight is..."
   171	- **Flex mechanism**: Annotate "content that can be skipped if time is tight" for flexible duration
   172	- **Key points structure**: `Key points: (1) Core insight (2) Data support (3) Strategic implication`
   173	
   174	### Notes Example
   175	
   176	```markdown
   177	# 03_strategic_path
   178	
   179	[Transition] Having clarified the problem and the opportunity, now comes the most critical part — our response path.
   180	
   181	We recommend a three-phase strategy. [Pause]
   182	
   183	Phase one: Focus. Over the next six months, concentrate resources on conquering the Eastern China market.
   184	[Data] Eastern China contributes nearly two-thirds of industry growth, [Benchmark] yet our penetration rate is only half of Competitor A's. [Pause]
   185	
   186	Phase two: Expand. Use Eastern China as a template, replicate to Southern and Northern China.
   187	Phase three: Scale. Leverage a digital platform for nationwide coverage.
   188	
   189	[Scan Room] The resource allocation for phase one is in the appendix — would you like me to walk through it now?
   190	
   191	Key points: (1) Focus-Expand-Scale three-phase approach (2) Data-backed Eastern China priority (3) 18-month full deployment
   192	Duration: 3 minutes
   193	Flex: [If time is tight, skip phase two and three details and go straight to financial impact]
   194	```
   195	
   196	---
   197	
   198	## MBB-level Quality Checklist Supplement
   199	
   200	### Content Level
   201	
   202	- [ ] **SCQA complete**: Overall follows Situation-Complication-Question-Answer structure
   203	- [ ] **Data contextualized**: Every data point has a comparison reference
   204	- [ ] **Conclusion first**: Every page's Takeaway Box has a one-sentence conclusion
   205	- [ ] **MECE principle**: Categorized analysis is mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive
   206	
   207	### Visual Level
   208	
   209	- [ ] **Color with intent**: Colors serve information delivery
   210	- [ ] **Ample whitespace**: Not crowded; information can "breathe"
   211	- [ ] **Visual hierarchy**: Conclusion > Arguments > Details, differentiated by font size/weight
   212	- [ ] **Brand consistency**: Gradient top bar and footer unified throughout
   213	
   214	### Notes Level
   215	
   216	- [ ] **Pyramid structure**: Every page is conclusion-first
   217	- [ ] **Stage markers complete**: [Pause] and [Scan Room] at key positions
   218	- [ ] **Flex content annotated**: Supports flexible duration

# 01_cover

Welcome to this data-driven overview of global CO₂ emissions. Today we'll trace the arc from historical emission growth through the dramatic shift in regional shares, to today's country-level dominance and per capita inequalities — all drawn from the Global Carbon Budget 2025 via Our World in Data.

Key points: (1) Deck covers fossil fuels & industry, 1750–2024 (2) Audience: policy analysts, climate negotiators, sustainability researchers (3) Tone: data-forward, analytical, accessible
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_global_emissions_growth

[Transition] Let's begin with the big picture: the long-run trajectory of global CO₂ emissions.

Global emissions from fossil fuels and industry have grown dramatically since the Industrial Revolution. Before industrialization, emissions were negligible. By 1950, the world emitted roughly 6 billion tonnes per year. By 1990, this had nearly quadrupled to over 20 billion tonnes. Today, global emissions exceed 35 billion tonnes annually. [Pause] While growth has slowed in recent years, emissions have not yet peaked. Fossil fuels continue to dominate the total, even as land-use change emissions have declined slightly.

Key points: (1) Pre-industrial emissions were negligible (2) 1950: ~6 Bt; 1990: ~20 Bt; 2024: >35 Bt (3) Growth slowing but no peak yet (4) Fossil fuels dominate
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 03_regional_share_shift

[Transition] While total emissions grew, the distribution of those emissions shifted profoundly.

In 1900, Europe and the United States accounted for more than 90% of global CO₂ emissions. By 1950, they still represented over 85%. But today, they account for less than one-third. [Pause] The most dramatic shift is the rise of Asia — led by China — which now produces roughly half of global emissions. This rebalancing has profound implications for climate negotiations and the question of historical responsibility versus current accountability.

Key points: (1) 1900: Europe + US >90% (2) 1950: Europe + US >85% (3) Today: Europe + US <33% (4) Asia now ~50% of global emissions
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_china_dominates_share

[Transition] Drilling down to country-level shares, one nation stands out.

China now emits more than one-quarter — roughly 31% — of global CO₂. The United States follows at approximately 13%, with India at ~8% and the EU-27 at ~6%. Together, these four account for nearly 60% of global emissions. [Data] Russia sits at ~5%, while Africa and South America each contribute only 3–4% — comparable to international aviation and shipping combined. [Benchmark] China's share is more than double that of the entire EU-27.

Key points: (1) China ~31%, rising but growth slowing (2) US ~13%, declining (3) India ~8%, rising (4) EU-27 ~6%, declining (5) Africa + S. America each ~3–4%
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_per_capita_inequality

[Transition] Total emissions tell only part of the story. Per capita figures reveal stark global inequalities.

The world's largest per capita emitters among populous countries are the United States, Australia, and Canada at roughly 14 tonnes per person — about three times the global average of 4.5 tonnes. [Data] At the other extreme, Chad and Niger emit approximately 0.1 tonnes per person. [Benchmark] The gap is enormous: a roughly 150× difference. [Pause] The average American emits in under two days what the average person in Niger emits in an entire year.

Key points: (1) US/Canada ~14 t, 3× world average (2) Chad/Niger ~0.1 t (3) 150× gap between highest and lowest (4) An American's 2 days = a Nigerien's year
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 06_per_capita_trends

[Transition] Let's look at the current per capita snapshot for key countries.

The United States and Canada lead at ~14 tonnes per person. China sits at ~9 tonnes — notable because despite being the largest total emitter, its per capita figure remains below the US. [Data] South Africa is at ~7 tonnes, the EU-27 at ~6, and the world average at ~4.5. The UK is even lower at ~4 tonnes. India remains very low at ~2 tonnes per person despite its massive population. Kenya is at ~0.4 and Chad/Niger at ~0.1. [Insight] This reframes the responsibility debate: total emissions and per capita emissions tell very different stories.

Key points: (1) US/Canada ~14 t (2) China ~9 t, below US despite largest total (3) India ~2 t, very low per capita (4) UK ~4 t, below world average
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_annual_change_2024

[Transition] What about the most recent year? The 2024 annual change map shows a mixed picture.

Many Western nations — including the US, much of the EU, and the UK — saw emissions decline. [Data] Meanwhile, Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations experienced increases. [Benchmark] Some countries in Central Asia, particularly the Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan region, saw particularly large increases exceeding 10%. [Pause] The overall pattern: gains in the developed West are being partially offset by rises elsewhere. This underscores that emission reductions in one region can be undermined by growth in another.

Key points: (1) US, EU, UK: declines (2) Russia, SE Asia, parts of Africa: increases (3) Central Asia: >10% increases (4) Mixed global picture
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 08_energy_mix_matters

[Transition] A critical insight emerges when we compare wealthy nations with similar prosperity levels.

France, the UK, and Portugal have much lower per capita emissions than Germany, the Netherlands, or the US. [Data] The UK is at ~4 tonnes while the US is at ~14. France is around ~5 tonnes. [Benchmark] The key driver? Energy mix. France derives roughly 70% of its electricity from nuclear power. The UK and Portugal have aggressively expanded renewables. [Insight] This proves that energy policy and technology choices can decouple prosperity from emissions. Similar living standards do not have to mean similar carbon footprints.

Key points: (1) France ~5 t, UK ~4 t vs US ~14 t (2) France: ~70% nuclear (3) UK/Portugal: high renewable share (4) Energy policy decouples prosperity from emissions
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 09_key_takeaways

[Transition] To conclude, five key takeaways frame the path forward.

First, global emissions exceed 35 billion tonnes per year and haven't peaked — the window for action is narrowing. Second, China is the largest annual emitter but per capita remains below the US, complicating simple narratives of responsibility. Third, historical responsibility is dominated by Europe and the US, which emitted over 90% in 1900 but now account for less than a third. Fourth, per capita gaps of 150× persist between richest and poorest nations — a profound equity challenge. And fifth, energy policy and technology choices can decouple prosperity from emissions. France and the UK prove it. [Scan Room] The question for negotiators is not whether responsibility is shared, but how to allocate it fairly across total emissions, per capita equity, and historical contribution.

Key points: (1) No peak yet, >35 Bt/yr (2) China largest total, per capita below US (3) Historical responsibility: Europe + US dominated (4) 150× per capita gap persists (5) Energy policy can decouple prosperity from emissions
Duration: 2.5 minutes

8. **Energy Mix Matters** — Grouped bar comparison + explanatory text: France/UK/Portugal (low) vs. Germany/US (high)
9. **Key Takeaways** — 5 conclusion cards: no peak yet, China's dual reality, historical responsibility, 150× gap, energy policy matters

All speaker notes are embedded in the PPTX file.
